Main.sentence: Netflix is an American ___E:subscription video on-demand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_on_demand#Subscription_models)___ ___E:over-the-top U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over-the-top_media_service)___ ___E:streaming U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media)___ service.
The service primarily distributes original and acquired films and television shows from various genres, and it is available internationally in multiple languages.

Launched in 2007, nearly a decade after ___E:Netflix, Inc. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix,_Inc.)___ began its pioneering ___E:DVD-by-mail U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD-by-mail)___ ___E:movie rental U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie_rental)___ service, Netflix is the ___E:most-subscribed video on demand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_streaming_media_services#Streaming_video_on_demand)___ ___E:streaming media U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media)___ service, with 301.6 million paid memberships in more than 190 countries as of 2025.   By 2022, "Netflix Original" productions accounted for half of its library in the United States and the namesake company had ventured into other categories, such as ___E:video game publishing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_publishing)___ of ___E:mobile games U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_game)___ through its flagship service.

As of 2025, Netflix is the ___E:18th most-visited website in the world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most-visited_websites)___ , with 21.18% of its traffic coming from the United States, followed by the United Kingdom at 6.01%, Canada at 4.94%, and Brazil at 4.24%.

Netflix was founded by ___E:Marc Randolph U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Randolph)___ and ___E:Reed Hastings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reed_Hastings)___ on August 29, 1997, in ___E:Scotts Valley, California U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotts_Valley,_California)___ .

Hastings, a computer scientist and mathematician, was a co-founder of ___E:Pure Software U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_Software)___ , which was acquired by ___E:Rational Software U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_Software)___ that year for $750 million, the then-biggest acquisition in ___E:Silicon Valley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley)___ history.
Randolph had worked as a marketing director for ___E:Pure Software U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_Software)___ after Pure Atria acquired a company where Randolph worked.

He was previously a co-founder of ___E:MicroWarehouse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MicroWarehouse)___ , a computer mail-order company, as well as vice president of marketing for ___E:Borland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borland)___ .

Hastings and Randolph came up with the idea for Netflix while ___E:carpooling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpool)___ between their homes in ___E:Santa Cruz, California U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz,_California)___ , and Pure Atria's headquarters in Sunnyvale.  ___E:Patty McCord U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patty_McCord)___ , later head of ___E:human resources U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_resources)___ at Netflix, was also in the carpool group.

Randolph admired ___E:Amazon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company))___ and wanted to find a large category of portable items to sell over the ___E:Internet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet)___ using a similar model.

Hastings and Randolph considered and rejected selling and renting ___E:VHS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VHS)___ as too expensive to stock and too delicate to ship.  When they heard about DVDs, first introduced in the United States in early 1997, they tested the concept of ___E:online DVD rental U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_DVD_rental)___ or sales by mail, by mailing a ___E:compact disc U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc)___ to Hastings's house in Santa Cruz.  When the CD arrived intact, they decided to enter the $16 billion ___E:Home-video U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_video)___ sales and rental industry.   [a] Hastings invested $2.5 million into Netflix from the sale of Pure Atria.
Netflix launched as the first DVD rental and sales website with 30 employees and 925 titles available—nearly all DVDs published.

Randolph and Hastings met with ___E:Jeff Bezos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Bezos)___ , whose ___E:Amazon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company))___ offered to acquire Netflix for between $14 and $16 million.
Fearing competition from Amazon, Randolph thought the offer was fair, but Hastings, who owned 70% of the company, turned it down on the plane ride home.
Not restricted to the size of a retail store, Netflix could offer hundreds of thousands of DVDs to customers in a ___E:long tail U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_tail)___ business model.
Early employee Cindy Holland compared the company acquiring DVDs to "shoveling coal in the side door of the house".

Initially, Netflix offered a per-rental model for each DVD but introduced a monthly subscription concept in September 1999.  The per-rental model was dropped by early 2000, allowing the company to focus on the business model of flat-fee unlimited rentals without due dates, late fees, shipping and handling fees, or per-title rental fees.  While customers enjoyed the convenience, more important to Netflix was that it did not have to store or ship those DVDs; subscribers' homes acted as warehouses.
The company secretly slowed deliveries to heavy users ("pigs"), to discourage them from quickly returning DVDs.

In September 2000, during the ___E:dot-com bubble U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble)___ , while Netflix was suffering losses, Hastings and Randolph offered to sell the company to Blockbuster for $50 million. ___E:John Antioco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Antioco)___ , CEO of Blockbuster, thought the offer was a joke and declined, saying, "The dot-com hysteria is completely overblown."   While Netflix experienced fast growth in early 2001, the continued effects of the dot-com bubble collapse and the ___E:September 11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ caused the company to hold off plans for its ___E:initial public offering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)___ (IPO) and to lay off one-third of its 120 employees.
DVD players were a popular gift for holiday sales in late 2001, and demand for DVD subscription services were "growing like crazy", according to chief talent officer McCord.

The company went ___E:public U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_company)___ on May 23, 2002, opening on ___E:NASDAQ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASDAQ)___ at US$15.00 per share with a sale of 5.5 million shares of ___E:common stock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_stock)___ .

In 2003, Netflix was issued a patent by the ___E:United States Patent and Trademark Office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Patent_and_Trademark_Office)___ to cover its subscription rental service and several extensions.
The company posted its first profit in 2003, earning $6.5 million on revenues of $272 million; by 2004, profit had increased to $49 million on over $500 million in revenues.
In 2005, 35,000 different films were available, and Netflix shipped 1 million DVDs out every day.

In 2004, Blockbuster introduced a DVD rental service, which not only allowed users to check out titles through online sites but allowed for them to return them at ___E:brick and-mortar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick_and_mortar)___ stores.
By 2006, Blockbuster's service reached two million users, and while trailing Netflix's subscriber count, was drawing business away from Netflix.

Netflix lowered fees in 2007.  While it was an ___E:urban legend U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend)___ that Netflix ultimately "killed" Blockbuster in the DVD rental market, Blockbuster's debt load and internal disagreements hurt the company.

On April 4, 2006, Netflix filed a ___E:patent infringement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement)___ lawsuit in which it demanded a ___E:jury trial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury_trial)___ in the ___E:United States District Court for the Northern District of California U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_Northern_District_of_California)___ , alleging that Blockbuster's online DVD rental subscription program violated two patents held by Netflix.

The first ___E:cause of action U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cause_of_action)___ alleged Blockbuster's infringement of copying the "dynamic queue" of DVDs available for each customer, Netflix's method of using the ranked preferences in the queue to send DVDs to subscribers, and Netflix's method permitting the queue to be updated and reordered.
The second cause of action alleged infringement of the subscription rental service as well as Netflix's methods of communication and delivery.
The companies settled their dispute on June 25, 2007; terms were not disclosed.

On October 1, 2006, Netflix announced the ___E:Netflix Prize U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix_Prize)___ , $1,000,000 to the first developer of a video-recommendation ___E:algorithm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm)___ that could beat its existing algorithm Cinematch, at predicting customer ratings by more than 10%.
On September 21, 2009, it awarded the $1,000,000 prize to team "BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos".
Cinematch, launched in 2000, was a system that recommended movies to its users, many of which might have been entirely new to the user.

Through its division ___E:Red Envelope Entertainment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Envelope_Entertainment)___ , Netflix licensed and distributed independent films such as Born into Brothels and Sherrybaby .

In late 2006, ___E:Red Envelope Entertainment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Envelope_Entertainment)___ also expanded into producing original content with filmmakers such as ___E:John Waters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Waters)___ .
Netflix closed Red Envelope Entertainment in 2008.

Hastings reportedly told ___E:Mynette Louie U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mynette_Louie)___ in the late 1990s that his goal was always ___E:streaming media U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media)___ , and that Netflix rented DVDs only to grow its customer base for streaming.
By the mid-2000s data speeds and bandwidth costs improved sufficiently to allow customers to download movies from the internet.
The original idea was a "Netflix box" that could download movies overnight, and be ready to watch the next day. By 2005, Netflix had acquired movie rights and designed the box and service.

But after witnessing how popular streaming services such as ___E:YouTube U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube)___ were despite the lack of high-definition content, the concept of using a hardware device was scrapped and replaced with a streaming concept.
In January 2007, the company launched a streaming media service, introducing ___E:video on demand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_on_demand)___ via the Internet.

However, at that time it only had 1,000 films available for streaming, compared to 70,000 available on DVD.   The service, then called "Watch Now", at first required ___E:Internet Explorer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Explorer)___ on a computer.

Hollywood studios (including ___E:20th Century Fox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Studios)___ , ___E:Sony Pictures U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Pictures)___ , ___E:MGM U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer)___ , ___E:Paramount Pictures U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures)___ , ___E:Universal Pictures U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures)___ , ___E:Warner Bros. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros.)___ , ___E:New Line Cinema U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Line_Cinema)___ and ___E:Lionsgate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Films)___ ) licensed ___E:second-run U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-run)___ content to the service, and did not expect it to threaten their existing lucrative relationships with ___E:cable television U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_television)___ .
In February 2007, Netflix delivered its billionth DVD, a copy of Babel to a customer in Texas.

In April 2007, Netflix recruited ___E:ReplayTV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ReplayTV)___ founder ___E:Anthony Wood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Wood_(businessman))___ , to build a "Netflix Player" that would allow streaming content to be played directly on a television rather than a desktop or laptop.

Hastings eventually shut down the project to help encourage other hardware manufacturers to include built-in Netflix support, which would be spun off as the ___E:digital media player U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_media_player)___ product ___E:Roku U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roku)___ .

In January 2008, all rental-disc subscribers became entitled to unlimited streaming at no additional cost. This change came in a response to the introduction of ___E:Hulu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulu)___ and to ___E:Apple U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.)___ 's new video-rental services.   [page needed] In August 2008, the Netflix database was corrupted and the company was not able to ship DVDs to customers for 3 days, leading the company to move all its data to the ___E:Amazon Web Services U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Web_Services)___ cloud.

In November 2008, Netflix began offering subscribers rentals on ___E:Blu-ray U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray)___ and discontinued its sale of used DVDs.  In 2009, Netflix streams overtook DVD shipments.

On January 6, 2010, Netflix agreed with ___E:Warner Bros. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros.)___ to delay new release rentals to 28 days after the DVDs became available for sale, in an attempt to help studios sell physical copies, and similar deals involving ___E:Universal Pictures U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures)___ and ___E:20th Century Fox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Fox)___ were reached on April 9.    In July 2010, Netflix signed a deal to stream movies of ___E:Relativity Media U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativity_Media)___ .

In August 2010, Netflix reached a five-year deal worth nearly $1 billion to stream films from ___E:Paramount U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures)___ , ___E:Lionsgate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Films)___ and ___E:Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer)___ .

The deal increased Netflix's annual spending fees, adding roughly $200 million per year. It spent $117 million in the first six months of 2010 on streaming, up from $31 million in 2009.  On September 22, 2010, Netflix launched in Canada, its first international market.
In November 2010, Netflix began offering a standalone streaming service separate from DVD rentals.

In 2010, Netflix acquired the rights to Breaking Bad , produced by Sony Pictures Television, after the show's third season, at a point where original broadcaster ___E:AMC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMC_(TV_channel))___ had expressed the possibility of cancelling the show. Sony pushed Netflix to release Breaking Bad in time for the fourth season, which as a result, greatly expanded the show's audience on AMC due to new viewers bingeing on the Netflix past episodes, and doubling the viewership by the time of the fifth season.
Breaking Bad is considered the first such show to have this "Netflix effect".

In January 2011, Netflix announced agreements with several manufacturers to include ___E:branded Netflix buttons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix_button)___ on the ___E:remote controls U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_control)___ of devices compatible with the service, such as ___E:Blu-ray players U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray)___ .
By May 2011, Netflix had become the largest source of Internet streaming traffic in North America, accounting for 30% of traffic during peak hours.
On July 12, 2011, Netflix announced that it would separate its existing subscription plans into two separate plans: one covering the streaming and the other DVD rental services.
The cost for streaming would be $7.99 per month, while DVD rental would start at the same price.
On September 11, 2011, Netflix expanded to countries in Latin America.

On September 18, 2011, Netflix announced its intentions to rebrand and restructure its DVD home media rental service as an independent subsidiary called Qwikster, separating DVD rental and streaming services.
On September 26, 2011, Netflix announced a content deal with ___E:DreamWorks Animation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Animation)___ .

On October 10, 2011, Netflix announced that it would retain its DVD service under the name Netflix and that its streaming and DVD-rental plans would remain branded together, citing customer dissatisfaction with the split.
In October 2011, Netflix and ___E:The CW U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_CW)___ signed a multi-year output deal for its television shows.
On January 9, 2012, Netflix started its expansion to Europe, launching in the United Kingdom and Ireland.
In February 2012, Netflix reached a multi-year agreement with ___E:The Weinstein Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weinstein_Company)___ .
In March 2012, Netflix acquired the ___E:domain name U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_name)___ DVD.com.
By 2016, Netflix rebranded its DVD-by-mail service under the name DVD.com, A Netflix Company .

In April 2012, Netflix filed with the ___E:Federal Election Commission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Election_Commission)___ (FEC) to form a ___E:political action committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee)___ (PAC) called FLIXPAC.

Netflix spokesperson Joris Evers tweeted that the intent was to "engage on issues like ___E:net neutrality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_neutrality)___ , ___E:bandwidth caps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandwidth_cap)___ , ___E:UBB U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usage-based_billing)___ and ___E:VPPA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Privacy_Protection_Act)___ ".
In June 2012, Netflix signed a deal with ___E:Open Road Films U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Road_Films)___ .
On August 23, 2012, Netflix and ___E:The Weinstein Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weinstein_Company)___ signed a multi-year output deal for RADiUS-TWC films.
In September 2012, ___E:Epix U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epix)___ signed a five-year streaming deal with Netflix.
For the initial two years of this agreement, first-run and back-catalog content from Epix was exclusive to Netflix.
Epix films came to Netflix 90 days after premiering on Epix.  These included films from Paramount, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer and Lionsgate.

On October 18, 2012, Netflix launched in ___E:Denmark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark)___ , ___E:Finland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland)___ , ___E:Norway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway)___ and ___E:Sweden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden)___ .

On December 4, 2012, Netflix and Disney announced an exclusive multi-year agreement for first-run United States subscription television rights to ___E:Walt Disney Studios U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Studios_(division))___ ' animated and live-action films, with classics such as Dumbo , Alice in Wonderland and Pocahontas available immediately and others available on Netflix beginning in 2016.  ___E:Direct-to-video U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct-to-video)___ releases were made available in 2013.

On January 14, 2013, Netflix signed an agreement with ___E:Time Warner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WarnerMedia)___ 's ___E:Turner Broadcasting System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turner_Broadcasting_System)___ and Warner Bros. Television to distribute ___E:Cartoon Network U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoon_Network)___ , ___E:Warner Bros. Animation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Animation)___ , and ___E:Adult Swim U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Swim)___ content, as well as ___E:TNT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT_(American_TV_network))___ 's Dallas , beginning in March 2013. The rights to these programs were given to Netflix shortly after deals with ___E:Viacom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_(2005%E2%80%932019))___ to stream ___E:Nickelodeon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickelodeon)___ and ___E:Nick Jr. Channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Jr._Channel)___ programs expired.
For cost reasons, Netflix stated that it would limit its expansion in 2013,  adding only one new market—the Netherlands—in September of that year. This expanded its availability to 40 territories.
Netflix had long closely analyzed its customers' preferences.

Watch Now gave the company real-time data on their behavior, such as scenes that customers replayed or skipped, or when they stopped watching a show.  In 2011, Netflix began its efforts into original content development.

In March, it made a straight-to-series order from ___E:MRC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MRC_(company))___ for the political drama ___E:House of Cards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Cards_(American_TV_series))___ , led by ___E:Kevin Spacey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Spacey)___ , outbidding U.S. cable networks.
This marked the first instance of a first-run television series being specifically commissioned by the service.

Netflix executives said that its customers' love of films by Spacey and show director ___E:David Fincher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Fincher)___ caused the company to acquire the show. Customers' tendency to ___E:binge watch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binge_watch)___ many episodes without stopping caused it to release all 13 episodes of the show's first season at the same time.  In November the same year, Netflix added two more significant productions to its roster: the comedy-drama Orange Is the New Black , adapted from ___E:Piper Kerman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piper_Kerman)___ 's ___E:memoir U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Is_the_New_Black:_My_Year_in_a_Women%27s_Prison)___ ,  and a new season of the previously cancelled Fox sitcom Arrested Development .

Netflix acquired the U.S. rights to the Norwegian drama Lilyhammer after its television premiere on Norway's ___E:NRK1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRK1)___ on January 25, 2012. Notably departing from the traditional broadcast television model of weekly episode premieres, Netflix chose to release the entire first season on February 8 of the same year.
House of Cards was released by Netflix on February 1, 2013, marketed as the first "Netflix Original" production.

Later that month, Netflix announced an agreement with ___E:DreamWorks Animation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Animation)___ to commission children's television series based on its properties, beginning with Turbo: F.A.S.T. , a spin-off of its film Turbo.

Orange is the New Black would premiere in July 2013; Netflix stated that Orange is the New Black had been its most-watched original series so far, with all of them having "an audience comparable with successful shows on cable and broadcast TV."

On March 13, 2013, Netflix added a ___E:Facebook U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook)___ sharing feature, letting United States subscribers access "Watched by your friends" and "Friends' Favorites" by agreeing.

This was not legal until the ___E:Video Privacy Protection Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Privacy_Protection_Act)___ was modified in early 2013.  On August 1, 2013, Netflix reintroduced the "Profiles" feature that permits accounts to accommodate up to five user profiles.

In November 2013, ___E:Marvel Television U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Television)___ and ___E:ABC Studios U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Signature)___ announced Netflix had ordered a slate of ___E:four television series U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel%27s_Netflix_television_series)___ based on the ___E:Marvel Comics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics)___ characters ___E:Daredevil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daredevil_(Marvel_Comics_character))___ , ___E:Jessica Jones U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Jones)___ , ___E:Iron Fist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Fist_(character))___ and ___E:Luke Cage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_Cage)___ .

Each of the four series received an initial order of 13 episodes, and Netflix also ordered a ___E:Defenders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defenders_(comics))___ miniseries that would tie them together. ___E:Daredevil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daredevil_(TV_series))___ and ___E:Jessica Jones U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Jones_(TV_series))___ premiered in 2015.    The Luke Cage series premiered on September 30, 2016, followed by Iron Fist on March 17, 2017, and The Defenders on August 18, 2017.   Marvel owner ___E:Disney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney)___ later entered into other content agreements with Netflix, including acquiring its animated Star Wars series Star Wars: The Clone Wars , and a new sixth season.

In February 2014, Netflix began to enter into agreements with U.S. internet service providers, beginning with ___E:Comcast U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comcast)___ (whose customers had repeatedly complained of frequent ___E:buffering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_buffer)___ when streaming Netflix), in order to provide the service a direct connection to their networks.

In April 2014, Netflix signed Arrested Development creator ___E:Mitchell Hurwitz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitchell_Hurwitz)___ and his production firm The Hurwitz Company to a multi-year deal to create original projects for the service.

On October 1, 2008, Netflix offered access to its service via a public ___E:application programming interface U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/API)___ (API).

The API was free and allowed commercial use.  In June 2012, Netflix began to restrict the availability of its public API.  Netflix instead focused on a small number of known partners using private interfaces, since most traffic came from those private interfaces.

Netflix presents viewers with recommendations based on interactions with the service, such as previous viewing history and ratings of viewed content.
These are often grouped into genres and formats, or feature the platform's highest-rated content.
Each title is presented with a thumbnail.
Before around 2015, these were the same ___E:key art U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_art)___ for everyone, but since then has been customized.
Netflix may select a specific key art for a thumbnail based on viewing history,  such as an actor or scene type based on genre preferences.
Some thumbnails are generated from video stills.
The Netflix recommendation system is a vital part of the streaming platform's success, enabling personalized content suggestions for hundreds of millions of subscribers worldwide.
Using advanced machine learning algorithms, Netflix analyzes user interactions, including viewing history, searches, and ratings, to deliver personalized recommendations for movies and TV shows.

The recommendation system considers individual user preferences, similarities with other users with comparable tastes, specific title attributes (genre, release year, etc.), device usage patterns, and viewing time. As users interact with the platform and provide feedback with their viewing habits, the recommendation system is able to adapt and refine its suggestions over time. Netflix uses a two-tiered ranking system, using the presentation of titles on the homepage for easy navigation to maximize user engagement.

This is done by organizing content into rows and ranking the titles within each row based on how much the user would be interested in it.  Netflix also uses A/B testing to determine what causes the biggest interest and engagement related to options concerning movie suggestions and how titles are organized.
Tags like "bittersweet", "sitcom", or "intimate" are assigned to each title by Netflix employees.
Netflix also uses the tags to create recommendation micro-genres like "Goofy TV Shows" or "Girls Night In".
Netflix launched "responsive recommendations", which display titles on the home page based on what its users are actively searching, in 2025.
